title: The loon
hook: he chased a loon on the pond that laughed and dived (Walden 12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ant war: red against black on the woodpile, and Thoreau stopping everything to watch. Your line was the small war. Did you catch a little fight and look at it from above? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

A calm afternoon in fall. The pond is flat as glass. Thoreau is out in his boat, and not far off sits a loon, a big black-and-white diving bird. He decides to get close. He paddles toward it. It dives. He stops and waits, scanning the water, guessing where it will come up. It surfaces somewhere else entirely, far off, sometimes behind him. And then it laughs. That long, wild loon call rolls across the water. So he picks a new direction and tries again. Then again. Today, a chase he was never going to win.
screen: `A CALM POND, A LOON.` → `IT DIVES.` → `IT LAUGHS.`

segments.voice: First, the game. In Brute Neighbors, Thoreau tells the chase move by move, and he calls it what it is: "a pretty game, played on the smooth surface of the pond, a man against a loon." Notice the word game. He isn't hunting it. He isn't trying to hurt it. He wants to outguess it, and he keeps losing. Second, the cleverness. He describes the loon picking the widest stretch of water to dive in, staying down long, swimming far underneath, and coming up where he least expected. This is the man who sounded the whole pond with a line and stone. He knows this water. And a bird still runs rings around him. Third, the laughter. Each time the loon comes up, it calls, and Thoreau hears the call as a laugh, wild and unearthly. He wonders if the bird is laughing at him. He doesn't sound offended. He sounds delighted. Fourth, the ending. Toward the end, the wind rises and a light rain begins, and Thoreau half-jokes that it's as if the loon had called on its god for help, and the god had answered. He gives up, and the loon is left where it was, out on the water, unbeaten. There's a kind of freedom in that ending. Not everything has to be caught, solved or won. Some things are better for being wilder than you are, and the best you can do is enjoy the game.
screen: `A MAN AGAINST A LOON.` · `IT COMES UP WHERE YOU DON'T LOOK.` · `A LAUGH ACROSS THE WATER.` · then, large: `THE LOON STAYS UNBEATEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let something wild outwit you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you can't control or predict: the weather, a cat, a small child, your own wandering mind. Let it be the loon. Watch it dive, and come up somewhere else. Notice the urge to chase it down. Then, for this one sit, let it win. If your attention wanders, don't drag it back hard. Smile at where it surfaced, and come back gently. The bell holds the time.
The loon. The bird that dived, surfaced far away, and laughed, in Thoreau's pretty game of a man against a loon. Today's word.
Your line: the laughing loon. Today, when something slips away from you that you can't control, try to enjoy the game instead of winning it, just once. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Brute Neighbors often enjoy the loon chase as a picture of meeting something wild with play rather than control, and of taking defeat with good humor.

notes: Confirm exact wording: 'It was a pretty game, played on the smooth surface of the pond, a man against a loon.'

Paraphrased: the loon's 'demoniac laughter', its 'unearthly howl', Thoreau's sense that it 'laughed in derision of my efforts', and the closing image of the east wind and drizzling rain as if the loon's prayer were answered. Confirm.
The text sets the chase on a calm October afternoon; the script says 'a calm afternoon in fall' to avoid a date claim beyond the text.
'He knows this water' is the narrator's emphasis, linking to the sounding in The Pond in Winter; trim if a reviewer prefers.
The description of a loon as a 'big black-and-white diving bird' is general natural history, not from the text.

Editor pass: removed the timeline claim that he sounded the pond later ('will one day'); practice no longer predicts the listener's mind ('and it will'); review line drops the invented 'on his knees'.
